en.html:
Confinement was generally governed by a trio: monotony, solitude, and the feeling of being shut in. Whatever the age or the world, that much would scarcely change.

Still, this could not go on indefinitely...

Apart from Lady Kanae's private reasons, GHQ must have had reasons of its own for keeping me inside its base. An army did not take prisoners for no purpose.

Keeping me caged and fed like a pet could hardly be the purpose in itself. Some approach would surely come.

But—it was taking its time.

In such days, anything that arrived to break the monotony was welcome. Whatever it might be.

幽閉生活というものはおおむね単調と孤独と閉塞の
三重奏に支配される。
　これは何処の世界のどんな時代でもまず変わらない
真理であろう。

　この状態がいつまでも続くとは思えないのだが……。
　俺がこうしてＧＨＱの基地内に囚われている事には、
香奈枝嬢の私的事情とは別にＧＨＱの事情がなくては
おかしい。無意味に虜囚を取る軍はない。

　その事情が、俺を愛玩動物よろしく檻に入れて餌を
与え続けること自体を目的としているとは考えられな
かった。
　必ず何らかのアプローチはしてくるだろう。

　しかし――それがなかなか訪れない。
　そんな日々において、単調さを崩してくれる要素の
到来は何であれ歓迎すべきものだった。

en.html:
When the Anglo-Saxons went into another country, they built <ruby>their own country<rt>・・</rt></ruby> there. So it was often said.

Not the same thing as overseas Chinese building a Chinatown. Those who had moved abroad for trade made a base, and a copy of home—a place of comfort. But that was the extent of it.

A Chinatown, both base and home, had a limit to its growth. Once the surroundings needed for their lives were sufficiently complete, there was no further expansion.

An Anglo-Saxon city expanded.

Without end.

In a country occupied by force, they destroyed or seized the local culture and civilization while building cities according to their own. In a trading partner, they actively exported their culture and civilization, until the city's appearance too became theirs.

Conquerors, in the true sense. The <ruby>British Commonwealth<rt>Great Britain</rt></ruby>, their parent state, controlled more than half the world politically. Its cultural territory was surely wider still.

Yamato, naturally, could not treat this as someone else's business. A hundred years had passed since the final overthrow of the Tokugawa regime, which had restricted foreign trade to protect domestic industry and culture. Now <ruby>automobiles<rt>motorcars</rt></ruby> passed through the streets, and <ruby>railways<rt>railroads</rt></ruby> connected the cities.

There were quite a few who feared these changes and sounded the alarm. <ruby>Ishima Sakon-no-Shougen<rt>Ishima Sakon-no-Shougen</rt></ruby>, author of The Argument for Selling the Nation, among them. More people, however, accepted the changes. Welcomed them. In one respect, they were lending a hand to the invasion of their own country.

And if matters had come to this, there was a reason for it. The Anglo-Saxons excelled at inventions founded on rationalism. In many fields, the convenience of their culture simply did not let other cultures catch up. What they made was fast, <ruby>huge<rt>big</rt></ruby>, strong.

Therefore people wanted it. Therefore it spread.

In the bluntest, plainest sense, with not one scrap of romance left to soften it, they were a race superior to the others.

Superior people with a superior scientific civilization. They believed in the justice of bringing that civilization to the backwaters; because it was justice, they did not hesitate.

The triumph of the Anglo-Saxon empire could hardly be called anything but inevitable.

ja.html:
アングロ・サクソン族は他国に進出すると、そこに
<ruby>自国<rt>・・</rt></ruby>を形成する――しばしばそう評される。

　それは華僑が中華街を造るのとは異なる。
　商業目的で他国に移住した彼ら華僑が築造する街は、
拠点であると同時に故郷の写し――安息の地であるが、
そこまでのものに過ぎない。

　拠点であり故郷である中華街は発展の限界を持つ。
　自分達の生活に必要充分な環境が完成すれば、それ
から更に規模を拡大していく事はない。

　アングロサクソンの都市は拡大する。
　際限なく。

　軍事的に占領した国では現地の文化文明を破壊また
は強奪しつつ自国の文化文明に沿って都市化する。
　交易関係を結んだ国へは、自国の文化文明を積極的
に輸出し、やがて都市の様相を自国化する。

　彼らは真の意味における征服者だ。
　アングロサクソン族の宗主国家といえる<ruby>大英連邦<rt>グレート・ブリテン</rt></ruby>は
政治的に世界の過半を制しているが、文化的な版図は
きっと更に広かろう。

　無論、大和にとっても他人事などではない。
　国内の産業と文化を保護するため諸外国との交易に
制限を掛けていた徳川政体が遂に打倒されて以来百年。
今や市街には<ruby>自動車<rt>モーターカー</rt></ruby>が行き交い、都市間は<ruby>鉄道<rt>レールロード</rt></ruby>が繋ぐ。

　そうした変化に危惧を抱き、警鐘を鳴らす人間も、
『売国論』を著した<ruby>石馬左近将監<rt>いしまさこんのしょうげん</rt></ruby>など少なからずいる。
　しかし、より多くの人々が変化を受け入れ、歓迎し、
一面において自国侵略の一助をなしているのだった。

　そしてそうなるからには、相応の理由が存在した。
　アングロサクソン族は合理主義に基づく発明に長け、
その文化の利便性は多くの方面で他文化の追随を許さ
ない。彼らが造る物は速く、<ruby>巨<rt>おおき</rt></ruby>く、強い。

　だからこそ求められ、普及する。

　最も身も蓋も味も素っ気もない意味において彼らは
他に優越する種族なのである。

　優秀なる彼らは優秀な科学文明を持ち、その文明を
僻地へもたらす正義を信じ、正義ゆえに躊躇わない。
　アングロサクソン帝国の覇業が成るのは必然と云う
べきであろう。

Perhaps a prisoner examining and criticizing everything without restraint had finally exhausted her patience? But that did not seem to be it.

Judging by her face, whether she was listening properly was itself in doubt.

嬢の反応はいつになく鈍い。
　生返事を寄越してくるばかりだった。

　捕虜でありながら遠慮もなく周囲を検分し批評する
態度が呆れを買ったのかとも思ったが、違うようだ。
　顔色を窺うに、そもそも話がまともに聞かれている
かどうかからして疑わしい。

Kageaki"Captain."
Kanae"..."
Kageaki"Are you perhaps feeling unwell...?"
Kanae"...Hm?"
Kanae"Ah, yes. I was thinking the same."
Kageaki"As I feared. Then please take care of yourself. For me, with nothing to do, the invitation was welcome. But that does not mean you must strain yourself on my account. No need to go to such lengths."
Kanae"Hm?"
Kageaki"Then we should return at once. To be safe, the army doctor—"
Sayo"Mr. Minato, we shall not need quite so much alarm just yet. She will be all right."
Kageaki"But—"
Sayo"My lady. Mr. Minato saw that your mind seemed to be elsewhere, and became concerned."
Sayo"The question, therefore, concerned your health... Is there something unsatisfactory about it?"
Kanae"...Ah."
Kanae"No, no, forgive me, Kageaki. As you see, there is plenty of life in me."
Kageaki"Truly?"
Kanae"Oh, far too much! Everywhere, full of life—quite a problem. Kageaki, would you like to see for yourself...?"

Kanae"Y-yes..."

Sayo"But consider the conditions, my lady. The time is three o'clock, the wind north-northwest, and the concentration of radio waves sixty-three percent. Normally, you would immediately give a monstrous bird-cry and begin dancing Mayim Mayim..."
Kanae"Yes, yes, I know! Give me one moment, will you? Time, correct. Wind, correct. Radio waves, correct."

Sayo"Well, she will recover in time, I expect."
Kageaki"Yes."
Sayo"That aside, Mr. Minato. I hear you met Professor Wolf?"
Kageaki"Yes. He invited me to his room, and we spoke briefly."
Sayo"What did you discuss? So far as there is no difficulty in disclosing it, of course."
Kageaki"...Let me see. The strongest impression, for the moment..."
Kageaki"The word 'grammar' was coming up again and again. Quite remarkably often."
Sayo"............"
Sayo"It seems the difficulty was on the listener's side."
Kageaki"My apologies."
Sayo"No, he is always like that. What kind of upbringing produced this, I could not tell you. But grammar does appear to have some special hold on him."
Sayo"Before anything else is said, there it comes: grammar, grammar—"
Kageaki"Attendant. On that point, let there be no misunderstanding."
Sayo"Hm?"
Kageaki"His interest is not in grammar. His interest is in demolishing it."

en.html:
There was an open space that looked like a drill ground.

I found I had stopped walking.

A group of a little over ten people was visible. Yet none looked ready to begin a drill.

Most were expressionless.
One had lost his expression.

The two things looked alike, but were different. In that one man, expression itself had gone missing. The others were deliberately concealing theirs.

The man whose expression had vanished had both arms bound. Those bonds were undone—or so I thought. Then his whole body was being tied to a stake.

　多くは無表情であった。

　一名は表情というものが欠落してしまったのであり、

縛り付けられていく。
